cues.txt: hey welcome to the shop today we're
building a go-cart now this isn't
designed to be the fastest or biggest
engine go card on youtube there are
other channels that do that
this was designed with a very specific
purpose in mind and that purpose is to
have a go-kart you can build with your
kids that's simple even for a beginner
and affordable i gave myself a few rules
when it came to this build
first of all i'm only going to use new
parts at prices available to the general
public
second nothing fancier than a chop saw
and a welding machine that means my
machine tools my tubing bender and cnc
are sitting the bench on this one and
last of all it needs to reasonably be
built by a beginner in the course of
three weekends which means we're going
to be buying a lot of off-the-shelf
parts to add to this cart now go cart
build starts with a frame and frames can
get really complex but when you boil it
down all you really need is a rectangle
in fact this entire frame was built out
of a single 20 foot length of one inch
square tubing
the side rails are cut to 4 feet long
which is about right to fit riders from
ages 7 to 12 which you know fits right
in with my kids
the front and rear of this rectangle are
going to be the axles first let's build
the front axle by attaching the spindle
kit that i got here
i'm just using some weld coupons to be
able to shim and prop everything up and
add a little bit of caster angle to the
front steering although at the speeds
this card will go it probably doesn't
really matter if they were just sitting
vertically straight up and down
to build the rear axle i just need to
attach two 5 8 inch bolts to either end
of this tubing now one of the bolts is
longer by one inch and that allows for
the brake drum and sprocket you'll see
us put on later
the extra tubing here is helpful to
align everything and have it sit flat
whenever you're welding on zinc plated
or galvanized material like these bolts
it's important to use enough ventilation
as well as a respirator to keep from
breathing in those fumes because they
can be pretty harmful now when i weld
these together the bolt head has a lot
more mass to it than the tubing itself
so i've set my machine up higher to be
able to penetrate into that bolt head
and i'll start my weld there and then
move over towards that tubing allowing
it to bridge the gap that way you can
get a sound weld that's penetrated into
the bolt without melting through my
tubing
i'll put the whole thing together making
sure that the rails are parallel and
using some switchable magnet squares to
hold the axles in place and centered
while i tack them on
notice how i'm moving around while i
weld this out and i'm welding the
phillip welds last these two things are
going to reduce distortion by quite a
bit and help everything to stay square
if you want to learn how to weld and
fabricate yourself to build cool
projects like this but have struggled to
make the traction you were hoping for
i've packaged all the information you
need in one place in my affordable
online courses
there are courses for each of the common
welding processes where i walk step by
step through telling you exactly what to
do in practice exercises you can find
all this link in the description below i
think it'll really help you out the
basic frame is done and i'm going to
test fit the wheels and spindles
and i'll show you how i put that drive
wheel and brake together in a minute
setting the seat and engine temporarily
in place this is starting to look like a
real cart and what we've done so far
could easily be done on your first day
of the build next i need to install some
cross members to mount the seat and the
engine even though this is a small
simple cart frame there's still a fair
amount of welding to do
well now is when it gets really fun so
everything went together pretty well i
made one small design change by putting
the seat rails front to back between two
cross members that way i can drill new
mounting locations whenever i want to
accommodate different size drivers
alright let me show you how i put
together the drive wheel now for wheels
and tires on this i use these wheel tire
combinations from harbor freight they
aren't necessarily designed for a
go-cart because this is going to have
such low loads of small riders and i'm
designing it to run at really low speeds
they should be okay for this application
but if you were to run something with
heavier riders or at higher speeds i'd
recommend getting a dedicated wheel tire
that's designed for a go-kart in order
to drive these wheels i need to take
apart the split rim and i'm going to use
the mounting bolts for that to attach a
drum brake and sprocket
i'm using a mini bike drum brake and
sprocket setup that i purchased but none
of the holes line up so i need to mark
this
to drill matching holes in the drum and
then i'm going to check and just make
sure my marks are centered at least by
eye these wheels have quite a bit of run
out on their own so i'm not concerned
about this being perfect but i wanted to
be as close as i can get
once i had some holes drilled in there i
used these steel spacers and some longer
bolts to assemble it together
okay so transferring the torque through
those spacers longer bolts that's not
going to be ideal but this is a
relatively low torque situation and it's
proven to be adequate as i've tested
this out to finish the chassis i need
several pieces cut out of some thick
sheet
and instead of spending all day with an
angle grinder i ordered them from an
online laser cutting service i just drew
them up in a free online cad package
uploaded them to send cut send it's a
service i've been using for years and i
get an instant quote click buy and they
show up a few days later ready to go and
install the first thing out of here that
i'll put in place is the engine mounting
plate which has some slots to allow me
to adjust the tension of the chain i'll
actually mount the engine to the plate
that way i can make sure that the
position side to side is in place and
everything's lined up rather than
welding these entire long seams an
intermittent weld should be strong
enough to hold it in this case let's get
to work on the steering for the steering
shaft i'm using some three quarter inch
round tubing
and attaching the pitman arm which i had
laser cut
to allow the steering shaft to rotate
i'm going to use some mounted bearings
now here's a little trick you might not
know
so typically when you buy round tubing
the outer diameter is actually a little
bit over the nominal size which is
frustrating if you want to use it for a
shaft but what i did is i bought 20
millimeter round bearings and 20
millimeters is just a little bit bigger
than three quarter inch of the shaft
which is going to leave a gap and cause
it to run out a little bit so it
wouldn't be good for rotating shaft but
for a steering shaft it works great i
had these plates laser cut to mount the
bearings and the first will attach to
the front frame rail
the geometry on the steering isn't
perfect but it works pretty good for
what we're building
now to mount the upper bearing we need
an upright support from the front of the
cross member i marked and cut a notch in
the tubing then mounted the bearing
plate to the other side i've just set it
at a 45 degree angle coming forward out
of the front crossmember
i need to attach a flange that i had
laser cut to mount the steering wheel i
just used a ruler to make sure
everything was aligned properly
now for the pedals
i had four of these tabs cut to mount
the pedals and drilled the hole out to
the exact size for the pedal shafts they
can be welded in place and the pedals
seem to work pretty good
for the cables i had these tabs cut to
weld to the frame rail they have a slot
to install the cable into now let's
install the brake it slides right over
the axle but i need something to keep it
from rotating as it's trying to stop the
drum from spinning i was going to use a
tab and a fastener welded in place but
instead i decided to just use a piece of
tubing and weld the actual brake itself
to that tubing keeps it simple and i'm
not going to remove this anyway
the wheel slides nicely over the brake
and i can mount the cable for testing
a shoulder screw and lock nut attaches
the front end of the cables to the
pedals
let's prep the engine i'm using a 79 cc
predator engine from harbor freight it's
their smallest predator but it should
have enough power for the size of ryder
and the low speeds that i'm expecting
out of this cart trying to keep it as
safe as possible
it sounds pretty good actually the first
thing i need to do is install a clutch
onto here now this is a centrifugal
clutch which will allow the engine to
spin freely when it's idling but when it
speeds up it'll engage the outer drum on
the clutch to be able to drive the
wheels this one has an 11 tooth sprocket
for number 35 chain that's the smallest
sprocket that i can get and i wanted the
smallest front sprocket because i'm
trying to keep the speed on this cart
pretty low
next i'll rotate the pull start to be
able to pull from the other direction
which will be the rear of the cart it's
going to put my label upside down but
it's going to be much easier to start
and while i'm at it over here i need to
add something to be able to
engage the throttle now i could have
made my own mount for the throttle
cables but i picked up this kit from go
power sports that will allow me to
attach a throttle cable right to this
engine it's pretty cool it has a bracket
that screws right in place as well as a
return spring and the ferrule that you
need to attach to your cable allowing it
to pull this lever here
now that everything's in place let's go
ahead and fire it up
well it's looking like where all systems
go i can go ahead and take it apart to
finish this thing up
i'm just cutting a small floorboard out
of this 18 gauge material i'm using a
plasma cutter here but you could just as
easily use an angle grinder to make this
cut
to hold the floorboard in place i'm
using short intermittent welds notice
how i started at the center of one end
worked my way out then up the side this
is going to help it stay flat
i ground down any sharp edges
gave the royal blue rattle can treatment
and i can put it back together
after the first test it was a little
faster than i was comfortable with so i
actually changed the rear sprocket from
a 60 tooth to a 72 tooth to slow it down
just a little bit and slowed down the
governor just a little more giving me a
top speed right around 15 miles per hour
my kids had a blast driving this thing
around and testing it out and seeing the
smiles on their face i couldn't help but
taking it for a little spin does this
not look so ridiculous
man driving that little cart makes me
want to build one for myself you know
maybe a vintage style cart get out the

files that i had cut out
by send cut send down in the description
you can see those as well as some other

and until next time weld safe and we'll
